title: Caterpillar Earnings Beat Estimates as Revenue Rises 17% to $20.68 Billion on Record Backlog
excerpt: Caterpillar posted its highest sales quarter ever and a record $78.1 billion backlog as data-center power demand surged, but a slim 1% beat and unchanged guidance sent shares down about 10%.
body:
• Caterpillar beat estimates in the third quarter: adjusted earnings rose 45% to $7.20 per share against $7.12 expected, and sales and revenues rose 17% to $20.68 billion against $20.58 billion expected.
  • It was Caterpillar's highest sales quarter ever, and strong order rates pushed the backlog up 96% to a record $78.1 billion — the fourth straight quarter of sequential backlog growth in all three primary segments.
  • Power & Energy led on data-center demand: segment sales rose 18% to $8.78 billion, with power-generation sales up 30% to $3.42 billion on turbines and large reciprocating engines.
  • Shares still fell about 10% pre-market: the beat was only about 1%, Caterpillar merely maintained full-year guidance, and adjusted operating margin of 20.6% included $128 million of tariff recoveries.

Caterpillar reported its highest sales quarter ever on Thursday, beating Wall Street estimates as demand for power equipment from data centers and steady construction spending lifted all three of its primary segments. The company announced third-quarter sales and revenues of $20.68 billion, up 17% from $17.64 billion a year earlier.

Volume and pricing did the work

Profit per share was $7.13, up from $4.88 a year earlier, and adjusted profit per share was $7.20, up 45% from $4.95, excluding restructuring costs of $41 million. Zacks reported the $7.20 figure beat its $7.12 consensus by 1.12%, with revenue also edging past its $20.58 billion estimate. The $3.04 billion year-over-year revenue increase reflected $2.21 billion of higher sales volume and $663 million of favorable price realization, with currency adding $58 million.

Operating profit rose 38% to $4.21 billion. The operating margin expanded to 20.4% from 17.3%, and the adjusted margin reached 20.6%. Results included $128 million of International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariff recoveries, a benefit investors are unlikely to treat as recurring. Enterprise operating cash flow was $4.4 billion, Caterpillar ended the quarter with $7.9 billion of enterprise cash, and it returned $2.0 billion to shareholders — $1.2 billion of buybacks and $0.7 billion of dividends in the release's rounded figures.

"Our third-quarter results reflect the durability of our end markets, with strong order rates and a record backlog. Our team continues to execute our strategic priorities in a dynamic environment, positioning us for a strong year."

— Joe Creed, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Caterpillar

Power & Energy is now the growth story

Power & Energy sales rose 18% to $8.78 billion, and segment profit rose 31% to $2.14 billion at a 24.4% margin. Power-generation sales jumped 30% to $3.42 billion, driven by turbines, turbine-related services and large reciprocating engines used in data-center applications. Oil and gas sales rose 13% and industrial sales 4%. Management said on the call that bringing additional capacity online remains the pacing factor for the segment, with large-engine orders extending into 2029 and turbine orders into 2030.

Construction Industries sales also rose 18%, to $7.98 billion, on higher equipment sales to end users and favorable pricing; segment profit rose 33% to $1.83 billion despite $252 million of unfavorable manufacturing costs, including freight. Resource Industries sales rose 15% to $4.62 billion, with mining, heavy construction and quarry sales up 22%, partly on dealer inventory changes, while rail sales fell 5%. Financial Products revenue rose 9% to $1.18 billion. Geographically, North America sales rose 24%, Latin America and Europe, Africa and the Middle East each rose 15%, and Asia/Pacific fell 2%.

Why the stock fell on a beat

The earnings surprise was the smallest in a year — about 1%, after beats of roughly 31% in the second quarter and 22% in the first — and Caterpillar maintained, rather than raised, its full-year outlook. Management expects full-year 2026 sales growth in the mid-to-high teens, moderate fourth-quarter growth, and an adjusted operating margin near the bottom of its target range excluding tariff recoveries, with about $2.2 billion of full-year tariff costs expected. For a stock priced for growth, that combination was not enough: shares fell about 10% in pre-market trading. The record $78.1 billion backlog says demand is real; the open question is how quickly Caterpillar can convert it without capacity and tariff costs eating the margin gain.
